keep: Applied science, done patiently in a field, can change the fate of nations.
lede: Frequently called the man who saved more human lives than anyone who has ever lived — and most people have never heard of him.
copy: An Iowa farm boy and plant pathologist, Borlaug spent the 1940s and 50s in Mexico. He crossbred thousands of wheat varieties. The goal was high-yielding, disease-resistant, short-stalked strains that could carry heavy heads of grain without toppling.

When famine threatened India and Pakistan in the 1960s, his wheat — paired with modern methods — roughly doubled harvests within years. Looming mass starvation turned into self-sufficiency. This was the Green Revolution, and it spread across Asia and Latin America. Estimates of the lives it saved from starvation run to a billion or more.

He won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970. He spent his remaining decades fighting hunger in Africa and defending agricultural science against critics, while acknowledging the environmental trade-offs of intensive farming. Borlaug is the quiet patron saint of the idea that applied science, done patiently in the field, can change the fate of nations.

bio.t: The Man Who Fed the World
bio.why: Hesser, an agricultural economist who worked alongside Borlaug in Pakistan, wrote the authorized biography with first-hand knowledge of the work. Warmly written and the fullest popular account.

contested: An authorized biography by a colleague is not an independent one. The 'saved a billion lives' figure is an estimate, and the Green Revolution's critics — on water depletion, fertiliser runoff, seed dependency and the concentration of gains among larger landholders — make arguments Hesser does not seriously engage. Both the achievement and the critique are real.
